power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Reverse Correlation and Agency
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: Using reverse correlation, we aim to explore the mental representation of agency. First, we will explore whether the mental representation of a person with high agency is perceived as more masculine and a face with low agency being perceived as more feminine. Second, we will explore dominance, attractiveness, trustworthiness, and perceived agency.
table.design_dependent_variables: The dependent variable will be the ratings of classification images created in the reverse correlation task (more information is provided in question 4).
table.study_design_overview:
Our experiment will have two phases:
We will run a reverse correlation task in which participants will have to pick which of two faces looks like they have either (a) high agency for one group or (b) low agency for another group. We will use the RCICR package on R to construct the CIs for high agency and low agency. To have a wider range of variability in the second phase of the task, we will also create multiple CIs from a random subset of 20 participants. 

In the second phase of the study, we will  ask a different group of participants to rate the CIs on gender, attractiveness, trustworthiness, dominance, and agency. We will use a linear scale going from 0 to 100.
table.statistical_tests:
For the statistical analysis, we will conduct a linear mixed model to look at the results from phase 2. We will run multiple mixed model analyses to look at the relationship between agency and each of the traits. We pre-register the most complex model here; however, it is possible that we may need to reduce the complexity of the model if it does not converge.

Model (using the lme4 syntax on r): 
Trait ~ 1 + Agency + (1 + Agency | Participants)
table.outliers_and_exclusions: We will include six attention check questions in the task. The questions will be explicitly asking the participants to press the left or right arrow. We will exclude all participants who miss more than 2 of the attention checks.
table.sample_size:
For Phase 1, we will have N=50 for each condition. There are no standard practices for a power analysis for reverse correlation, so we matched the standard sample sizes from past studies.  

For Study 2, N=156. We ran a power analysis using MorePower (ver. 6.0.4) to determine our sample size based on the main effect of gender perception. While MorePower cannot handle linear mixed-effect models, we opted to use a t-test between two dependent means (matched pairs), specifically powering (at 80%) assuming a small effect size d of 0.2 for a one-tailed test.
table.additional_comments: We will do some exploratory analyses to look at different mixed models, the specific pixels used to gather information in the task and create z maps of the relevant face areas. We will also include questionnaires to capture particioants' gender biases and will check for any effect os biases on CI ratings.

table.research_questions:
Using reverse correlation, we aim to explore the mental representation of agency. First, we will explore whether the mental representation of a person with high agency is perceived as more masculine and a face with low agency being perceived as more feminine. Second, we will explore other traits such as dominance, attractiveness, mood, etc. 

This is a replication of a previous study using the same methods, but changing one aspect of the stimulus: namely, using a male face as the base image in the task.

In the second phase of the study, we will  ask a different group of participants to rate the CIs on different traits, including which gender identity they perceive them to have. We will use a linear scale going from 0 to 100.

table.text: The CIs from Study 2a were rated as more masculine A main effect of participant gender was found only for masculinity ratings (b = 5.40, 95% CI [0.61, 10.20], t(434) = 2.21, p = .027): the CIs of male participants were rated as more masculine than those of female participants overall.

Turning to interaction effects, we found a significant interaction between study and participant gender for agency ratings: in Study 1a, the CI from female participants was rated as having more agency than the CI from male participants (b = 8.85, 95% CI [0.73, 16.96], t(432) = 2.14, p = .033).

live_data_statements: In Study 1a, participants completed a traditional reverse correlation task with an androgynous base image, selecting the face that looked more or less agentic depending on their assigned condition.
In the image generation phase, participants are presented with two stimuli and asked to select the one that better fits a target representation [12].
As a post-hoc analysis, we also split our participant group in phase 2 of each study by gender and tested whether their CIs differed.

Emotional Faces Database (B) Base image used for Study 2B: MNES from the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces Database (C) Example stimulus from Study 1A (D) Example stimulus from Study 2A (E) For every trial, participants had to choose which of two faces looked more [less] in control of actions and their consequences (F) We averaged the noise from all the images selected by the participants and superposed it back onto the base image to create our Classification Images (CIs).
Participants were recruited via Prolific from a United Kingdom sample.
A total of 100 participants were recruited, with 50 participants randomly assigned to each of the two AoA conditions (high vs. low).
Participants were redirected to Jatos via Prolific.
Participants were then provided with the instructions: "Your job is to choose the person who looks more [less] in control of what they do and what happens as a result."

text.text: As people move through their social environment, they constantly make assumptions about others' abilities and personalities, often relying on personal characteristics as cues.
One such characteristic is gender.
One robust pattern is that people tend to attribute agency to masculine individuals.
Here, we asked whether this relationship holds when approached from the opposite direction: is the representation of agency itself gendered?
Using reverse correlation, we conducted two studies to construct a visual representation of agency and examine its associated attributes.
In Study 1a, participants completed a traditional reverse correlation task with an androgynous base image, selecting the face that looked more or less agentic depending on their assigned condition.
In Study 1b, a separate group of participants rated the resulting classification images (CIs) from Study 1a; agency was represented not as masculine, but as feminine, attractive, and trustworthy.
Study 2a replicated Study 1a using a masculine base image instead, and in Study 2b, agency was represented as neither masculine nor feminine, but again as trustworthy and attractive.

Together, these studies suggest that agency is not represented in a gendered way, but rather through attractiveness and trustworthiness, indicating that agency may be best captured by socially desirable traits more broadly, rather than by gender.
When interacting with our environment, we constantly evaluate whether or not we are in control.

This experience of being in control of our actions (and subsequent effects) has been termed the sense of agency (SoA) [1] https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?imEV8V  [2] https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?imEV8V  [3].

text.text: Importantly, we also attribute agency to others (attribution of agency, AoA).
Agency is often described as a masculine trait [4] https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?TKK71V  [5].

text.text: While men are represented as strong agents, women are represented as dependent on others.
The gender bias around AoA has consistently been noted and observed across different disciplines.
In biologyhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?0klX2y discussions of anatomy and evolution have been shaped by stereotypes of passive females and active males [6] ,  [7].
text.formatted: In biology, discussions of anatomy and evolution have been shaped by stereotypes of passive females and active males <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?0klX2y">,</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: In the media, women have been represented as docile and passive while men are described as adventurous and agentic [8].
text.formatted: In the media, women have been represented as docile and passive while men are described as adventurous and agentic <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Psychologicallyhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?KUenXC although gender stereotypes are shifting, the conceptualisation of AoA as masculine still stands and is moderated by factors such as sexual orientation, relationship status, and specific agency traits [5] ,  [9].

text.text: Beyond descriptive stereotypinghttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?FPhrFf biases in AoA carry direct social consequences: because agency is one of the two fundamental dimensions along which people evaluate others (alongside warmth/communion [10] , how much agency an observer attributes to someone shapes judgments of their competence, leadership potential, and credit for shared outcomes.

text.text: When women act in agentic ways, this agency is often either underattributed to them (e.g.: "Matilda effect" [11]) or attributed but socially penalized (backlash effects [9]).

text.text: Gender bias in AoA is therefore not a peripheral phenomenon but leads to tangible downstream effects on who is seen as a leader, an innovator, or a hero, and who is not.
The question remains, however, how strongly agency and gender are associated on an implicit level and whether masculinity is an integral part of our conception of agency..

In order to address these questions, we suggest a new approach to investigate gender biases in AoA: Rather than using traditional self-report and behavioural measures, we instead use reverse correlation to investigate the association of agency and gender..
Reverse correlation is a data-driven method that allows one to visualize the perceptual content of the mental representation of some target concept, such as agency [12].
text.formatted: Reverse correlation is a data-driven method that allows one to visualize the perceptual content of the mental representation of some target concept, such as agency <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: In other words, this method allows us to flip the question around: rather than asking participants whether they perceive masculinity to showcase agency, we explore whether their representation of agency involves masculinity.

text.text: The paradigm has already been used to explore gender biases by testing for example whether feminists are represented as more masculine [19] or leaders were represented in a less feminine manner than non-leaders [20].
text.formatted: The paradigm has already been used to explore gender biases by testing for example whether feminists are represented as more masculine <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[19]</ref> or leaders were represented in a less feminine manner than non-leaders <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[20]</ref>.

text.text: As outlined above, our aim is to investigate whether the mental representation of agency is gendered.
A standard reverse correlation set-up consists of two phases.
In the image generation phase, participants are presented with two stimuli and asked to select the one that better fits a target representation [12].
text.formatted: In the image generation phase, participants are presented with two stimuli and asked to select the one that better fits a target representation <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: For example, when the researcher is aiming to capture the mental representation of trustworthiness, they might ask participants to pick the face that looks more trustworthy.
A key point of the task is that all the stimuli are based on the same base image (often an average face computed from a database of face stimuli) and only differ in the noise superimposed.

By averaging the noise from all the selected stimuli, one can create a Classification Image (CI), which contains the visual information used by participants to form their representation of the construct.

In the image rating phase, a different group of participants is asked to rate the CIs on dimensions of interest, which serves to quantify the distinctive features of the CI -that is, the mental representation captured in the image generation phase.
Here, we ran two studies that consist of two parts each.
In the image generation phase of Study 1a and Study 2a we asked participants to classify faces based on whether they have either high or low agency.
The studies only differed in the gender of the base image.
While in Study 1 we used an average of male and female faces that looked nevertheless more feminine, in Study 2 we used a clearly masculine base image.
In studies 1b and 2b, we asked a second group of participants to rate the classification images of the image generation phase based on personality characteristics, including perceived gender.
As a post-hoc analysis, we also split our participant group in phase 2 of each study by gender and tested whether their CIs differed.
We expected that the CI resulting from high AoA would look more masculine than that resulting from low AoA.
Furthermore, we expected that the high AoA CI would be represented as more attractive and trustworthy than low AoA CI.

text.text: Procedure.
Participants were redirected to Jatos via Prolific.
We first presented them with the chance to read the letter of information to provide their consent.
Participants were then provided with the instructions: "Your job is to choose the person who looks more [less] in control of what they do and what happens as a result."

text.text: We also provided them with an example of having control as a person flipping a switch to turn the light on.
Participants were instructed to use the right and left arrow keys to make their choice.
There was no time limit for each trial, but we noted that the faces might look very similar to each other but are indeed different.
We asked participants to make the choice based on their initial intuition and to stay fully concentrated.
The order of the stimuli was randomized per participant.
We also included 6 attention check trials to our task.
For these trials, the images on the screen would have an arrow pointing either left or right.
Participants had to select the corresponding side.
Participants were excluded if they missed more than 2 attention checks.
You can also find the scripts for the task and analysis, as well as the stimuli on our OSF repository.
We used the generateCI function from the RCICR package to compute the classification images.
We created CIs for the full sample of each condition, as well as CIs based on the gender of the participant.

To assess how meaningful each participant's classification image (CI) was, we computed the information value (infoVal) for each individual CI using the computeInfoVal2IFC function from the RCICR package.
The infoVal indicates how different a participant's responses were from what would be expected by chance, using a comparison against a randomly simulated dataset (Brinkman et al., 2019).

text.text: Because infoVal is expressed on a z-score scale, a value of 1.96 or higher indicates that a participant's CI was significantly more informative than random noise, at the conventional threshold of p = .05.
We used this cutoff to identify a subset of participants (hereafter referred to as the high infoVal group) whose individual CIs carried significant informational content.
We also generated z-maps for two CIs: the high AoA CI for the low AoA CI, and the CI derived from the high infoVal group of the high AoA condition.

A z-map visualizes, pixel by pixel, which regions of a CI significantly predicted participants' judgments; higher z-scores at a given pixel indicate that variation in that pixel was more strongly associated with participants' ratings.

The present study investigated whether the mental representation of agency is gendered.
Extensive prior work has shown that facial or trait masculinity predicts perceptions of greater agency [4] https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?lDia5u  [5].
text.formatted: Extensive prior work has shown that facial or trait masculinity predicts perceptions of greater agency <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?lDia5u">,</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: The present study inverted this direction, asking instead whether agency is associated with a representation of masculinity: does an agentic mental representation itself carry a masculine appearance?
Our findings suggest that, while perceptions of masculinity may predict an increase in AoA, AoA does not predict perceptions of masculinity.

Across two studies using different base images, our findings show that agency is not strictly represented as masculine, but rather depends on the facial features of the base image and the gender of the viewer.
In Study 1a, when the stimulus we used as the base of our task had feminine-rated features, agency was actually represented as feminine.
Although using a masculine base image in Study 2a did attenuate these results, high agency was represented as more masculine than low agency but equally masculine to the base image.
The masculinity and femininity of high agency CIs were also dependent on the gender of the viewer for both studies.
The findings of Studies 1a and 2a may therefore be attributable to the base image used for the stimuli.

Although technically gender-neutral, the base image used in Study 1a was rated as more feminine than masculine and participants might have integrated the feminine features from the base image into their representation of agency.
However, the role of gender in agency perception might be too complex to manifest in a simple pattern and depends on factors such as the viewer's gender.

Another possible explanation for the AoA agency CI being represented in a feminine manner in Study 1a could be linked to the finding that gender representations in faces that do not always align with those captured through verbal or behavioral measures [23] https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?gBTPUS  [24].
text.formatted: Another possible explanation for the AoA agency CI being represented in a feminine manner in Study 1a could be linked to the finding that gender representations in faces that do not always align with those captured through verbal or behavioral measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[23]</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?gBTPUS">,</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[24]</ref>.

text.text: One example is that androcentrism (the tendency to attribute masculinity as the default when no gender information is given) does not generalize to face perception.
When asked to pick the face that looks most like a typical person, the CI turned out looking feminine [25].
text.formatted: When asked to pick the face that looks most like a typical person, the CI turned out looking feminine <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[25]</ref>.

text.text: There are many possible explanations for this finding, such as the softening of facial traits due to the averaging process.
The absence of androcentrism in facial representations could partially explain why our high agency CIs looked more feminine than masculine.

Because CIs have a tendency to look feminine, even when in contexts where we expect gender-neutrality or masculinity, it is possible that the mental representation of agency does not look masculine in spite of the verbal associations of masculinity.
Based on our results, it seems to be that agency is not represented in a gendered manner but in a socially desirable way.
That is, instead of masculinity, we found that trustworthiness and attractiveness were represented in agency.
The high agency CIs from Studies 1a and 2a were both rated as more attractive and trustworthy than the low agency CI and the base image.

This pattern suggests that, at least in the context of our study, perceivers may be relying on general evaluative dimensions-how good, competent, or likeable a face appears-rather than on gender-typical features when inferring agentic qualities.

This finding is consistent with the literaturehttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?P3SS9h where agency is discussed to be a desirable traithttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?P3SS9h especially when it comes to choosing a mate [26] ,  [27] ,  [28].
text.formatted: This finding is consistent with the literature, where agency is discussed to be a desirable trait, especially when it comes to choosing a mate <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[26]</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?P3SS9h">,</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[27]</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?P3SS9h">,</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[28]</ref>.

text.text: Given that agency is already understood as a socially desirable characteristic, it follows that a face designed to convey high agency would also be perceived as more attractive, since desirable traits tend to cluster together in social perception.

This interpretation goes in line with the"what is good is beautiful" theory [29] https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?gGwpy7 which claims that traits judged as positive are bundled together in our perception of attractiveness.
text.formatted: This interpretation goes in line with the"what is good is beautiful" theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[29]</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?gGwpy7">,</ref> which claims that traits judged as positive are bundled together in our perception of attractiveness.

text.text: Hence, agency being a positive trait to have, it seems to be bundled with trustworthiness (another positive trait) and represented by an attractive face.
The increased representation of trustworthiness and attractiveness in both studies (more strongly so in Study 1a) may also be tied to our finding that high agency is not associated with masculinity.

Using both reverse correlation and other models of facial feature attributionshttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?YjlpJ1 trustworthiness has repeatedly been linked to femininity while dominance has been linked with masculinity [30] https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?YjlpJ1  [31] ,  [32].
text.formatted: Using both reverse correlation and other models of facial feature attributions, trustworthiness has repeatedly been linked to femininity while dominance has been linked with masculinity <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[30]</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?YjlpJ1">,</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[31]</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?YjlpJ1">,</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[32]</ref>.

text.text: As the CIs of high agency portrayed a strong trustworthiness representation and a lack of dominance representation the link between dominance/trustworthiness and gender might be driving our findings regarding agency being represented in a feminine manner.

Arguably, the representation of agency as trustworthy and attractive (and thus feminine) might be overriding the representation of agency as masculine, suggesting that even though masculinity is associated with agency in explicit trait judgments, the implicit/visual representation of agency inherits trustworthiness's feminine coding rather than dominance's masculine coding.
Moreover, the gender of participants played an important role in their mental representation of agency.
We found a gender congruency effect: when the base face's gender matched that of the participants from Studies 1a and 2a, that gender representation was exaggerated in the CIs of high agency.
In Study 1a, when the base face was rated as high on femininity, the CI of high agency looked more agentic for the female group than the male group.
In Study 2a, when the base face was high on masculinity, the CI of high agency looked more agentic for the male group than the female group.
Interestingly, in Study 2a, female participants also rated the high agency CI (built from the masculine base image) as more dominant.
This suggests that when the underlying face already had masculine features, women's mental representation of agency incorporated dominance as well.
The gender congruency effect could also be discussed in terms of in-and out-group representations rather than a gender-specific phenomenon.
Reframing the gender congruency effect described above, when the base face characterized the in-group of the participant, the CI also looked to be higher on agency.
This finding could be an aspect of self-projection or in-group projectionhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?N1yeRO onto one's representation of high agency [33] ,  [34].
text.formatted: This finding could be an aspect of self-projection or in-group projection, onto one's representation of high agency <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[33]</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?N1yeRO">,</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[34]</ref>.

text.text: In other words, participants might have projected both themselves and their perception of their in-group onto their representation of high agency.
Our results, however, cannot differentiate between an in-group representation of agency and a gender-congruent representation of agency.
For this reason, future studies could explore how self-projection, in-group projection, or gender representations influence one's representation of agency.
It's also important to mention that the reverse correlation method has been criticized for having inflated type 1 errors [35].
text.formatted: It's also important to mention that the reverse correlation method has been criticized for having inflated type 1 errors <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[35]</ref>.

text.text: Our task includes some measures to ensure that our results are not due to a type 1 error.
First of all, we included two opposing conditions (High Agency vs Low Agency), which provides a control through comparison between conditions.
We also included a comparison of the CIs to those of the base image, which informs us that the ratings we get on the CI go beyond the main features of the base image.

We have also taken some of the suggestions by Cone et al [35] to make sure that our results are not due to general statistical effects: we designed the task to have 500 trials in Studies 1a and 2a, which is shown to lead to higher infoVals and computed the infoVals at the individual level and ran a correlation analysis on the z-maps of the group CI and high infoVal CIs to ensure that the group CIs are informative.
text.formatted: We have also taken some of the suggestions by Cone et al <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[35]</ref> to make sure that our results are not due to general statistical effects: we designed the task to have 500 trials in Studies 1a and 2a, which is shown to lead to higher infoVals and computed the infoVals at the individual level and ran a correlation analysis on the z-maps of the group CI and high infoVal CIs to ensure that the group CIs are informative.

text.text: We also included attention checks which ensured that the participants were attending to the stimuli throughout the task, even if they end up with a lower infoVal.
Our study aimed to investigate whether agency is represented by masculinity.

Taken togetherhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?rurb5a our findings suggest that the relationship between agency and masculinity is not symmetrical: while masculinity reliably predicts perceptions of agency [4] ,  [5], the reverse does not hold: we do not associate agency with masculinity.
text.formatted: Taken together, our findings suggest that the relationship between agency and masculinity is not symmetrical: while masculinity reliably predicts perceptions of agency <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?rurb5a">,</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>, the reverse does not hold: we do not associate agency with masculinity.

text.text: Instead, the representation of agency was coded through trustworthiness and attractiveness rather than masculinity.

Given that AoA shapes real-world judgments of leadership and credit [9], this dissociation raises the question of where the masculine-agency bias actually takes hold (whether in explicit trait attribution, in visual representation, or in the mapping between the two) a question future work combining reverse correlation with explicit trait measures could directly address.

text.text: More broadly, as gender is a social construct, identifying which features are and are not intrinsically represented as gendered helps clarify how gender itself is defined and constructed [36].
